procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Punjab High Court (Circuit Bench) at Delhi dated March 13, 1964, in Criminal Revision No. 30-D of 1964 and Criminal Misc. No. 63-D of 1964, transferring the complaint to the Court of the Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi for disposal.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. The Punjab High Court (Circuit Bench) at Delhi initially transferred a criminal complaint to the Court of the Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi (order dated March 13, 1964). 
2. The appellant then applied to the Punjab High Court under s. 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code praying that the Criminal complaint may be transferred to a Magistrate of competent jurisdiction.
3. The learned Chief Justice of the Punjab High Court dismissed this application on March 12, 1965, on the ground that the High Court had no power to review its previous order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, who had initially moved for the transfer of the case, argued that the High Court had no power to transfer a case pending in the Court of a Magistrate to the Court of the Additional Sessions Judge. The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal the High Court's orders. The Supreme Court allowed Criminal Appeals 86 and 88 of 1965, set aside the order of the Chief Justice of the Punjab High Court dated March 13, 1964, and directed that the criminal case be transferred to the Court of any other 1st Class Magistrate stationed at Delhi to be selected by the learned Chief Justice of the Punjab High Court under s. 526(1) (iv) of the Criminal Procedure Code. Criminal Appeal 87 of 1965, against the order of the High Court refusing to review its order of transfer dated March 13, 1964, was dismissed as infructuous.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the competence to transfer a case pending in the Court of a Magistrate to the Court of an Additional Sessions Judge for trial.

facts: The central issue is whether a High Court has the legal authority to transfer a criminal case from a Magistrate's Court to an Additional Sessions Judge's Court for trial.
The appellant, who had initially requested the transfer, later argued that the High Court lacked the power to make such a transfer.
The respondents contended that the High Court did possess this power.
law: The primary legal provision under consideration is Section 526(1)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which allows a High Court to transfer a case from a criminal court subordinate to it to "any other such Criminal Court of equal or superior jurisdiction."

A related legal principle is that a Court of Sessions generally cannot take "cognizance of any offence as a court of original jurisdiction" unless the accused has been formally committed to it by a Magistrate.
application: The Court first analyzed the plain language of Section 526(1)(ii), noting that it explicitly permits the transfer of a case to a court of "superior jurisdiction." Since a Sessions Court is superior to a Magistrate's Court, the text of the law appears to grant this power.
The Court then addressed the appellant's main argument: that a transfer without a formal commitment order would violate the rule that a Sessions Court cannot take original jurisdiction without one.

The Court rejected this argument by drawing a distinction between a Sessions Court "taking cognizance" on its own and receiving a case via a transfer order from the High Court. It reasoned that when a case is transferred, the criminal proceedings have already been initiated by the Magistrate.

The Sessions Court's authority to hear the case comes directly from the High Court's transfer order, not from the commitment process. Therefore, the Sessions Court is not taking cognizance in the traditional sense but is simply proceeding with a trial as directed by a higher court.
The Court also found it would be "incongruous" if a High Court could transfer a case to itself for trial but not to a Court of Session, another superior court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court, by a majority, held that the High Court is competent under Section 526(1)(ii) of the Code to transfer a case from the Court of a Magistrate to the Court of a Sessions Judge. The transfer order from the High Court provides the necessary jurisdiction, and a separate commitment order is not required in such a scenario. (Note: There was a dissenting opinion arguing that the High Court has no such power without a proper commitment having been made).

issue.issue_text: Whether the Court of an Additional Sessions Judge has jurisdiction to proceed with the trial of a criminal case transferred to it by the High Court from a Magistrate's court, in the absence of an order of commitment.

facts: The High Court transferred a criminal case from a Magistrate's court to the Court of an Additional Sessions Judge.
This transfer was made without an order of commitment, which is the usual procedure for a case to move from a Magistrate to a Sessions Court for trial.
law: Section 193(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code generally prohibits a Sessions Court from taking "cognizance of any offence as a court of original jurisdiction" unless the accused has been committed to it by a Magistrate.
Section 526(1)(ii) of the Code grants the High Court the power to transfer a case from a criminal court to another criminal court of "equal or superior jurisdiction."
application: The Court reasoned that the bar in Section 193(1) applies when a Sessions Court takes original cognizance, meaning it is the first court to initiate proceedings for the trial.
However, in this situation, the Sessions Court was not taking original cognizance. The proceedings had already been initiated in the Magistrate's court.

When the High Court transfers a case, the receiving court (the Sessions Court) is not deciding whether to initiate proceedings; it is simply obligated to proceed with the trial as directed by the High Court's transfer order.
The Court concluded that the act of receiving a transferred case is different from taking cognizance. Therefore, the requirement of a commitment order under Section 193(1) does not apply.
The broad power of transfer given to the High Court under Section 526 allows it to move a case to a superior court, like the Sessions Court, and this power is not limited by the commitment procedure.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court is competent to transfer a case from a Magistrate's court to a Sessions Court even without a commitment order. Consequently, the Additional Sessions Judge had the jurisdiction to proceed with the trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the competence to transfer a case pending in the Court of a Magistrate to the Court of an Additional Sessions Judge for trial.
appellant_arguments: The provisions of s. 526(1)(ii) of the Code should be construed narrowly to only permit transfers between courts of the same level (e.g., Magistrate to Magistrate).
Transferring a case from a Magistrate to a Sessions Court would create procedural difficulties, as the Code does not specifically provide the procedure to be followed in such a trial.
This omission of a specific procedure implies that such a transfer is not legally intended or permissible.
respondent_arguments: The plain language of s. 526(1)(ii) explicitly gives the High Court the power to transfer a case from a Magistrate's court to any other criminal court of equal or superior jurisdiction, which includes a Sessions Court.
The absence of a specifically prescribed procedure in the Code does not invalidate or make the transfer illegal when the power to transfer is clearly conferred by the statute.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Court of an Additional Sessions Judge has jurisdiction to proceed with the trial of a criminal case transferred to it by the High Court from a Magistrate's court, in the absence of an order of commitment.
appellant_arguments: There is no express provision in the Code that empowers a Court of Session to take cognizance of a case as a court of original jurisdiction when it is transferred directly by a High Court.
In the absence of a committal order or an express provision, the Court of Session is incompetent to take cognizance and proceed with the trial.
respondent_arguments: The Additional Sessions Judge gains jurisdiction to proceed with the trial directly from the transfer order made by the High Court.
The procedure to be followed in such a trial should be that of a warrant case, as contemplated by s. 526(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court is competent under section 526(1)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to transfer a case from the Court of a Magistrate to the Court of the Sessions Judge. The omission of a specifically prescribed procedure for the trial of such a transferred case does not render the transfer illegal or invalidate the power conferred by the statute.
obiter: The omission of a specific procedure to try a case withdrawn by the High Court from the Court of a Presidency Magistrate does not negate the High Court's power to withdraw such a case under the clear words of the statute.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court is competent under s. 526(1)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to transfer a case from a Magistrate's Court to a Court of Session. The explicit statutory power to transfer a case to a court of superior jurisdiction is not negated by the mere omission of a specifically prescribed procedure for the trial in the transferee court. The jurisdiction of the Sessions Court to try the case is conferred directly by the High Court's transfer order, rendering a separate order of commitment unnecessary.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation (Plain Meaning Rule): The court relied on the clear and explicit language of s. 526(1)(ii) which confers the power of transfer on the High Court.

Reasoning by Analogy: The court compared the omission of procedure in the present case to a similar omission in s. 526(2) concerning cases withdrawn from a Presidency Magistrate's Court, concluding that in both instances, the absence of a specified procedure does not nullify the explicitly granted statutory power.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the omission of a specific procedure for trial implies a lack of power to transfer was rejected. The court held that an explicit grant of power is not invalidated by a procedural omission in the statute.

The contention that a Court of Session is incompetent to take cognizance without a committal order was unsuccessful because the court found that jurisdiction is conferred directly by the High Court's transfer order itself.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the plain language of s. 526(1)(ii) unambiguously confers power on the High Court to transfer a case from a Magistrate to a court of superior jurisdiction, which includes a Court of Session.
The court agreed that the absence of a specifically prescribed procedure in the Code does not make the transfer illegal when the power to transfer is clearly conferred by the statute.
The court's reasoning supports the respondent's position that the Additional Sessions Judge gains jurisdiction to proceed with the trial directly from the transfer order made by the High Court.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning ensures that the High Court's substantive power to order a transfer for the purpose of a fair and impartial trial is not defeated by a procedural lacuna or omission in the Code of Criminal Procedure.
